entries.notes: Completed cleanly. Incumbent improved the 8-row iso holdout from 36.712076s to 32.205814s with zero wrong answers, a modest 1.14x aggregate speedup. The profile keeps default preprocessing, disables UF symmetry and eq-bridge, uses theory_phase=polarity, prop_budget=1000, and prop_interval=128. NEQ016 is a real tuned-LLM2SMT gap as well as a Z3 gap: tuned LLM2SMT solves locally in about 21.5s while Primo did not solve before interruption at 92s. The tuned reference did not use LLM2SMT's finite-domain value-precedence option for this improvement; the recorded tuned profile uses UF symmetry, four preprocessing passes, equality bridge, and EUF propagation thresholds.

summary.correctness: Three distinct soundness bugs found and fixed during implementation, all the same root cause (a node's own signature can be rehashed and rediscovered congruent more than once, so naively resolving to 'current identity' and linking through that silently drops a bridge fact from the explanation): (1) ProofForest::explain only alias-resolved the top-level query, not obligations produced mid-walk; (2) re-coalescing an already-aliased member needs its old alias materialized into a real tree edge first, not overwritten; (3) the same applies to the canonical side and to direct-equation endpoints, plus a has_incoming_edge_ tracker was needed since a self-rooted node can already have a real incoming edge a naive parent_[node]==node check would miss. After all three fixes: hand-derived Example 22/23 tests pass, and the 180-step randomized backtracking oracle test passes under both default and ASAN/UBSan builds.

Working hypothesis, not confirmed: materialize()'s retroactive reversals happen outside the normal Union-driven growth pattern Lemma 13's amortized O(log n) bound depends on ('each reversal at least doubles the reversed edge's tree size'), and may violate that invariant. Not investigated further this session.

summary.bug: has_incoming_edge_ (added to gate ProofForest::coalesce_into_structural_class's cheap alias fast path, see the previous run's fix 3) only covered real union_nodes e_prime targets, not coalesce_into_structural_class's own fast-path alias targets. summary.profile_finding: perf record on NEQ016_size7 (20s bounded window, process did not terminate pre-fix) showed ~76% of all samples inside ProofForest::explain and its two NCA-search helpers: aux_find 38%, explain 19%, nearest_common_ancestor 13%, explain_along_path 6%. Every other function, including all of FlatCongruenceClosure's own merge/backtrack machinery, was individually under 0.1%. This is the inverse of every other mode's profile.
summary.bug_1_tree_depth: Lemma 13's amortized O(log n) reversal bound requires every Union to reverse the smaller side's path. reoriented-proof-forest's direct-equation caller already does this (chooses e/e' by live class_size_ before calling union_nodes). coalesce_into_structural_class's fallback branch (member vs canonical, chosen by lookup-table arrival order) and materialize (always reverses the alias source's path) had no size discipline at all, and live class_size_ stops being an accurate proxy for real tree size once fast-path aliasing exists (an aliased member inflates its live class without adding real tree depth). Fixed by adding ProofForest's own size_ tracking and making union_nodes itself swap which physical node plays e vs e' when the caller's choice disagrees with tracked size -- sound regardless of caller intent, since a tree edge's label proves its two endpoints equal however it is attached. Verified via direct instrumentation: max real tree depth stayed at 46 after 200,000 union_nodes calls post-fix, versus growing unboundedly before.
summary.bug_2_memoization: Fixing bug 1 alone did not fix NEQ016_size7 (still did not finish in 30s). Further instrumentation showed seed_and_resolve (explain's alias-chain walker) called over 1 billion times in 15 seconds against only ~5,000 top-level Explain calls in that window; alias-chain hop count itself stayed flat (max 1 hop, confirming bug 1's fix was working and this was a separate issue). The auxiliary union-find already deduplicates repeat tree-edge congruence obligations reached via explain_along_path's NCA walk (the mechanism Section 5.2's own complexity argument depends on), but nothing deduplicated repeat alias-bridge obligations reached via seed_and_resolve -- a coalesced node's bridge obligations were pushed once per referencing obligation, not once per Explain call, and structural-class coalescing routinely produces a few popular hub canonical nodes referenced many times within one call. Fixed with the same generation-stamped mark pattern already used for aux_generation_/ancestor_generation_ in this file (seed_marks_/seed_generation_): a node's bridge obligations are now pushed at most once per top-level Explain call.
summary.result: NEQ016_size7 standalone: 180s+ (not finishing) -> 3.67s, in line with default (3.11s) and reoriented-proof-forest (3.05s). 334-file sweep (10s timeout): solved 232->248 (PAR2 9.329->8.643); reoriented-proof-forest in the same post-fix run was 254/8.279, so the gap closed from 27 files behind to 6 files behind, and file-level divergence dropped from 43/334 to 20/334. Not yet a clear win over reoriented-proof-forest, but no longer a clear, broad loss.
summary.verification: Unit tests and a freshly-configured ASAN/UBSan build pass after each of the two fixes. A 2000-instance fuzzsmt-against-z3 round against the ASAN/UBSan build came back 2000/2000 PASS after each fix (0 crashes, 0 disagreements) -- confirms neither fix introduced a new soundness issue, including the size-based e/e' swap in union_nodes, which changes the internal tree shape for every mode sharing that function (reoriented-proof-forest included) but was argued sound because a tree edge's label does not depend on which physical node carries it; the existing full test suite (including reoriented-proof-forest's own tests) still passes unchanged.

artifacts.note: fuzz-results/qf_lra-smoke/ (round 1, pre-fix) and fuzz-results/qf_lra-smoke2/ (round 2, post-fix) -- local, not committed (gitignored).

summary.round1_pre_fix: 300 cases: 257 UNSUPPORTED_INPUT (sat refs), 38 UNSUPPORTED_INPUT (unsat refs), 5 CRASH, 0 PASS. Nearly universal UNSUPPORTED_INPUT traced to a real bug: build_times/build_divide recognized a literal `*`/`/` operand by pattern-matching the raw S-expression before ever calling build_term, so a let-bound alias of a literal (e.g. `(let ((c 3)) (* c x))`) was never recognized as a coefficient, even though it resolves to one after build_term's own let-binding lookup. fuzzsmt let-binds nearly every literal in its QF_LRA output, so this rejected almost all fuzzer-generated input.
summary.fix: Rewrote build_times/build_divide to build both operands via build_term first (which already resolves let-bindings, definitions, and nested arithmetic that constant-folds via TermManager's own mk_plus/mk_times), then check the *resulting* term's TermKind::Rational-ness -- simpler than the original raw-syntax-matching design, not just more correct. The top-level bare-numeral-atom fast path was also simplified to a plain util::Rational::parse(expr.atom) check inside build_term's Atom branch, since compound literal forms (`(- lit)`, `(/ lit n)`) are now handled correctly by the ordinary build_minus/build_divide recursive-build path with no special-casing needed.
summary.round2_post_fix: Same 300-case campaign re-run after the fix: 251 UNSUPPORTED_INPUT (sat refs), 17 UNSUPPORTED_INPUT (unsat refs), 20 PASS (unsat/unsat), 3 PASS (sat/sat), 6 CRASH, 3 TIMEOUT (5s budget). Zero wrong-answer disagreements against z3 across both rounds -- the critical soundness property held throughout.
summary.crash_triage: All 6 crashes share one signature: AddressSanitizer stack-overflow inside primo::smtlib::SExpr's recursive copy constructor, triggered purely by S-expression nesting depth, before any theory-specific code runs. Confirmed NOT QF_LRA-specific: reproduced the same fuzzer settings against QF_UF (100 cases) with zero crashes, but QF_UF's fuzzsmt output at these settings averaged ~136 lines/file versus QF_LRA's ~534 lines/file (fuzzsmt's arithmetic term generator produces deeper nesting) -- QF_LRA just happens to hit the same latent, pre-existing, theory-agnostic parser-robustness gap more often, not a new one. Out of scope for this milestone; tracked as a follow-up (would need converting SExpr copying and/or build_term's recursion to be iterative, or adding an explicit depth limit).
summary.remaining_unsupported_input: Manually sampled several post-fix UNSUPPORTED_INPUT cases: overwhelmingly the known, explicitly-tested disequality gap ("QF_LRA disequality (a negated Real equality) is not yet supported") -- fuzzsmt generates many equalities that end up negated somewhere in the formula. This is an intentional, documented Milestone 1 scope boundary (case-splitting for disequality isn't implemented yet), not an unknown bug.

summary.result: 82 files, 10s timeout: 45 solved (19 sat, 26 unsat), 37 timeout, 0 unsupported, 0 wrong (out of 74 files with a checkable :status). PAR2 805.5. Solve rate is heavily family-dependent, not uniform: 6 families 100% solved within 10s (DTP-Scheduling, keymaera, meti-tarski, sal, spider_benchmarks, check), 4 families 0% solved (2017-Heizmann-UltimateInvariantSynthesis, LassoRanker, latendresse, tropical-matrix), the rest partial. The 0%-solved families are exactly the ones with large formulas (invariant synthesis, lasso ranking termination arguments) -- consistent with the earlier single-file investigation (2026-07-24 disequality entry) showing genuine but slow search progress without theory propagation.
summary.significance: Zero wrong answers and zero unsupported across a completely different, much larger and more structurally realistic distribution than fuzzsmt's generated formulas is meaningful independent soundness/coverage evidence -- this is the first time QF_LRA has been evaluated against anything other than synthetic fuzzer output or hand-written unit tests. The solved-rate split by family reinforces (does not merely repeat) the propagation-importance finding: it's not that QF_LRA is broadly too slow, it's specifically the large/complex families that stall, matching the theory-propagation-starved-search hypothesis rather than e.g. a uniform per-atom overhead problem.

Implemented in two steps: (1) PreparedLraTheory dedupes tableau slack variables by exact LinearPolynomial content (a prerequisite -- propagation needs atoms to share a slack, which essentially never happened under the old one-slack-per-atom scheme), (2) OnlineLraPropagator scans atoms sharing a just-asserted atom's slack and eagerly propagates entailed true/false atoms via new LraTableau::upper_bound()/lower_bound() accessors.

summary.result: First run (before the bug fix below): 255 PASS, 16 TIMEOUT, 229 CRASH -- a real regression, all crashes the SAME new bug (CaDiCaL abort 'external reason clause must contain the propagated literal'), not the pre-existing SExpr recursion issue. Root cause: OnlineLraPropagator::notify_backtrack cleared its entire reasons_ map unconditionally on every backtrack, including entries for literals that remained assigned after backtracking to new_level -- CaDiCaL's conflict analysis (explain_external_propagations) legitimately asked for such a literal's reason later and got an empty clause back. Fixed by only erasing a reasons_ entry when its literal's var is actually popped from the propagator's own var_trail_ (mirroring how assigned_ is already scoped), leaving pending_ (undelivered candidates only, always safe to drop) as the sole thing cleared unconditionally. Re-ran the same 500-case campaign after the fix: 424 PASS, 69 TIMEOUT, 7 CRASH, 0 WRONG -- all 7 crashes individually reconfirmed (via direct stack-trace inspection) as the identical pre-existing SExpr stack-overflow already triaged in the Milestone 1 entry, not a new issue.
summary.significance: This is the second real bug (after the let-bound-literal and real-equality-misclassification bugs in Milestone 1) caught by the project's fuzz-gate discipline rather than shipped -- a subtle backtracking/reason-clause-lifetime bug that unit tests alone (which don't exercise deep, varied DPLL(T) backtracking patterns) would have been very unlikely to catch. Reinforces that the merge-gate tier (500 cases) is pulling real weight for propagator-touching changes, exactly as it did for Milestone 3a.

summary.significance: A genuinely neutral result, reported honestly rather than spun: same-slack bound propagation alone did not move this sample's hardest families. This is consistent with (not contradicting) the milestone's design scope -- propagation here only relates atoms sharing the *exact same* tableau slack, and the hardest families (invariant synthesis, lasso ranking) likely need either scale-invariant polynomial matching (atoms like x<=5 vs 2x<=10 currently get separate slacks) or the paper's stronger row-based/interval propagation across different variables (both explicitly out of scope for 3b) to see a similar win. The milestone's value is independently confirmed at the unit-test level instead (qf_lra_solver_tests.cpp's same_slack_propagation_* tests show propagation measurably avoiding SAT decisions on hand-built cases where atoms do share a slack) -- this benchmark sample apparently just doesn't have much of that specific pattern in its hardest files.

summary.result: Two bugs found and fixed in sequence, each caught before landing cleanly: (1) SExpr's recursive copy ctor/destructor and parser.cpp's recursive parse_one both replaced with iterative algorithms (Frame-stack based) -- fixed all 7 crashes from the prior Milestone 3b fuzz-gate entry (confirmed: same corpus files, re-run after this fix alone, all 7 stopped crashing). (2) Frontend::build_term's own recursive descent turned out to be a SEPARATE, deeper bug: even with SExpr fixed, a synthetic 200000-deep nested `+` still segfaulted (Release build) via TermManager::mk_plus's call chain through build_term/build_ite/etc, and ASAN's larger stack frames meant it was actually THIS bug, not the SExpr one, causing all 7 of the Milestone 3b fuzz-gate crashes under ASAN. Fixed via TermBuilder, a continuation-passing iterative driver. Caught a genuine design mistake in the first TermBuilder attempt during local testing (before it ever reached fuzzing): only child-descent was trampolined, not continuation delivery, so long chains still recursed natively via direct k(...) calls -- fixed by routing every continuation invocation through resume() too. Local verification (500 QF_LRA + 300 QF_UF fuzzsmt cases, ASAN/UBSan): 0 crashes, 0 wrong answers, both up from a 7/500 crash rate before the fix. A campaign-tier (3000+ case) QF_LRA fuzz gate was additionally submitted to the llm2smt-slurm cluster (job 113267) for independent confirmation at scale, per standing project guidance that campaign-tier fuzzing belongs on Slurm rather than run locally.
summary.significance: Removes a theory-agnostic crash class that had been present (and repeatedly rediscovered/re-triaged as 'pre-existing, out of scope') since Milestone 1's fuzz gate. Also a notable methodological point: the Milestone 3b fuzz-gate's crash count (~7/500, stable across several campaigns) was consistently attributed to the SExpr issue by inspection of the stack trace signature, but was actually dominated by the build_term recursion once examined under ASAN's stack-frame overhead -- a reminder that superficially-similar 'stack-overflow' signatures can have different root causes, and that fixing the first plausible cause doesn't guarantee the crash is gone (confirmed here only by re-running the exact same crashing files after each fix in isolation).

summary.result: Two real infrastructure bugs found and fixed while getting this campaign running (neither is a Primo correctness issue): (1) the first submission (job 113267, against the pre-M4 commit) completed in ~1 second with 'fuzzsmt is not installed; skipping external fuzzing' -- slurm_prepare_benchmark_workspace.py only builds the primo binary, not the fuzzsmt/z3 tooling scripts/fuzz_external.py depends on, so that job silently did nothing rather than actually fuzzing. Fixed by running `make contrib-fuzzsmt contrib-z3` remotely and setting up a .venv-yinyang venv with yinyang/z3-solver installed for opfuzz/typefuzz. (2) The very next slurm_prepare_benchmark_workspace.py sync (to pick up the M4 commits) then clobbered that remote contrib/local with the LOCAL machine's contrib/local via rsync (contrib/local wasn't excluded), reintroducing the same failure via a different symptom (fuzzsmt's wrapper script has a host-specific absolute jarfile path baked in at install time) -- fixed by excluding contrib/local and contrib/src from the rsync (commit 605caad), then re-provisioning remotely. A remaining minor PATH gap (opfuzz specifically resolves via bare PATH lookup, not the TYPEFUZZ override) was caught and fixed with a small supplementary single-task job (113328) rather than restarting the whole array. As of this entry, job 113319's core fuzzsmt shards (0-5) are running (confirmed genuinely executing, not instantly completing); yinyang shards (7-8) already completed cleanly (14/14 seeds valid, 0 bug triggers); opfuzz (113328) is running. Full campaign results to be recorded in a follow-up entry once complete.

summary.result: 500/500 cases: 324 PASS, 176 TIMEOUT, 0 CRASH, 0 WRONG, 0 UNSUPPORTED_INPUT. Job took 18m28s wall-clock (vs. ~4m for the analogous Gaussian-elimination/row-propagation merge-gate runs) and the timeout rate (176/500, ~35%) is notably higher than those runs' (~25-32/500, ~5-6%).

benchmark.suite: benchmarks/qf-lra-stratified-sample.txt (237 files, up to 15/family across all 17 QF_LRA corpus families)

artifacts.note: Remote results/qf-lra-solver-compare-113461/{primo,z3,cvc5}.csv and *-summary.csv pulled back locally (not committed -- large per-file detail, reproducible from the manifest).

summary.result: Solved (of 237): primo 102 (43%), z3 167 (70%), cvc5 150 (63%). PAR2 (10s timeout): primo 2799, z3 1531, cvc5 1885. Zero 3-way disagreements on concrete sat/unsat answers across all 237 files -- Primo's answers, where it produces one, are never wrong relative to either reference solver. Per-family breakdown is NOT uniform: Primo fully matches z3/cvc5 (15/15 or 2/2) on keymaera, meti-tarski, sal, spider_benchmarks, check, and is close on DTP-Scheduling (11 vs 15/13); on 2017-Heizmann-UltimateInvariantSynthesis, LassoRanker, and tropical-matrix all three solvers struggle roughly equally (these are genuinely hard for everyone, matching earlier quick-eval findings). But on TM (4 vs 15/14), sc (4 vs 13/12), uart (3 vs 13/12), 2019-ezsmt (3 vs 10/7), tta_startup (8 vs 14/13), and miplib (1 vs 6/5), Primo is specifically and substantially behind while z3/cvc5 mostly solve these within the same 10s budget. Spot-checking TM/uart's primo failures: purely TIMEOUT (not wrong-answer, not error, not unsupported) -- and the cases Primo DOES solve in these families solve fast (1.9-8.8s), suggesting a threshold effect (some difficulty/size crossing point) rather than uniform slowness.
summary.significance: First genuine empirical evidence of WHERE Primo is behind, rather than inferring from a 17-file one-per-family sample dominated by the 'hard for everyone' families. This broader, family-stratified sample reveals a *different*, more tractable-looking set of gap families (TM, sc, uart, 2019-ezsmt, tta_startup, miplib) that the earlier narrow sample never surfaced -- these are prime candidates for follow-up investigation (e.g. profiling what's actually slow on a representative TM/uart timeout case) before further committing to items 2/3/4's engineering directions, since none of those (row-based propagation, SOI-Simplex) were evaluated against this specific, more informative family set.

pending: Root-cause investigation of the TM/sc/uart/2019-ezsmt/tta_startup/miplib timeout gap -- not yet profiled to determine what's actually the bottleneck (Simplex search itself, preprocessing overhead, something else).

entries.scope: Merge-gate-tier (500-case) fuzz smoke test for the LraTableau::pivot()/set_soi_direction() allocation fix (commit 04a6c73), following up on item 0's empirical baseline by profiling (perf) the 3 most dramatic Primo-timeout-but-z3/cvc5-instant cases it surfaced: tmp/QF_LRA/sc/sc-21.induction3.cvc.smt2, tmp/QF_LRA/uart/uart-18.induction.cvc.smt2, tmp/QF_LRA/TM/p5-zenonumeric_s5.smt2. perf showed 50-60% of runtime in malloc/free/GMP-allocation machinery, with pivot()'s per-affected-row combine step (a fresh std::unordered_map<LraVarId, Rational> built and torn down for every row touched by every pivot) as the dominant contributor; set_soi_direction() had the identical pattern. Fixed by replacing both with a reused member vector, sort-merged instead of hashed (a first attempt that just reused an unordered_map member did NOT help -- unordered_map is node-based, so every element is its own heap allocation regardless of container reuse; confirmed by re-profiling). Run on llm2smt-slurm per the standing policy that all fuzzing, including merge-gate smoke checks, is dispatched to Slurm rather than run locally.

summary.result: 500/500 cases: 471 PASS, 29 TIMEOUT, 0 CRASH, 0 WRONG, 0 UNSUPPORTED_INPUT.
summary.significance: No wrong-answer disagreements against z3 and no crashes from this hot-path pivot rewrite -- the highest-risk part of this change (same trail/undo machinery item 4's SOI-Simplex work already flagged as its own highest-risk surface). summary.three_bottleneck_classes: Class A (latendresse): 0 decisions, 1 check() call -- one conjunctive LP that never finishes, so SAT-side heuristics are irrelevant there. Class B (clock_synchro 1,515 decisions / 8,997 pivots / 13.9s; miplib pp08a-12000 4,564 / 8,314 / 13.9s): ~1.5 ms per pivot. Class C (DTP-Scheduling constraints-tempo-width-30: 60,750 decisions, ZERO conflicts, 63,021 check calls, 7,182 pivots, 19.5s): ~320 microseconds per decision with no learning at all.
summary.perf_flat_profile: On constraints-tempo-width-30: LraTableau::pivot 31.4% self; allocator ~42% (_int_malloc 10.5, _int_free 7.9, malloc 5.8, cfree 5.2, malloc_consolidate 5.2, unlink_chunk 4.3, gmp_default_allocate 1.5); GMP copy/init ~12% (__gmpn_copyi 5.6, __gmpz_init_set 3.4, __gmpq_clear 1.6); actual bignum arithmetic ~5% (__gmpz_mul 1.4, __gmpq_mul 1.0, __gmpz_gcd 0.8, __gmpn_gcd_1 0.7, __gmpz_divexact_gcd 0.5, __gmpq_aors 0.5); rebuild_occurs_in_index 1.3%.
summary.corrects_prior_conclusion: This contradicts the conclusion recorded under roadmap item 0's follow-up (2026-07-26) that what remained after the container fixes was inherent mpq_class GCD canonicalization that 'no container-level fix can remove'. Measured, canonicalization/GCD is under 2% and ALL real bignum arithmetic is ~5%; ~54% is malloc/free plus copying of TINY numbers. The values are small, the representation is expensive -- which makes a small-rational (int64/int64 with GMP fallback) fast path the single largest available lever, not a dead end.
summary.tableau_shape: Share of prepared rows that are a single-variable slack (row = c*x): latendresse/ecoliFBAyicesTest-500 3,161/4,555 (69%); TM/p6-zenonumeric_s5 1,311/1,378 (95%); miplib/pp08a-12000 262/400 (66%); sc-17 462/1,185 (39%); uart-17 526/1,446 (36%); tta_startup 84/584 (14%); LassoRanker/selectSort 653/9,469 (7%); clock_synchro 5/264 (2%); DTP-Scheduling/constraints-tempo-width-30 0/3,932 (0%, average row exactly 2.00 and max row 2 -- a pure difference-logic problem in QF_LRA clothing). Dutertre & de Moura Section 2 introduces slack variables only for compound polynomials; Primo allocates one per distinct polynomial including bare variables, and because polynomial keys are exact-content matches, '(<= 0 r1)' and '(<= r1 1000)' land on two DIFFERENT slacks for the same variable.
summary.fill_in: Rows densify 3-5x during search. constraints-tempo-width-30: average row 2.00 -> 3.7-8.9, max row 33, max occurs_in 2,127. clocksynchro_2clocks: 2.75 -> 8.1-14.3, max row 34, max occurs_in 174. ecoliFBAyicesTest-500: 3.39 -> 7.9-23.9, max row 961, and fewer than 2,000 pivots in 30+s (>15 ms per pivot). Since pivot() costs |occurs_in(entering)| * |row(leaving)| rational operations, and none of Bland/Dantzig/SOI prices a pivot by its cost, fill-in is currently unopposed.
summary.design_output: docs/qf-lra-heuristics.md proposes six items in priority order: H2 small-rational fast path in util::Rational; H1 direct bounds for single-variable atoms plus scale-canonical polynomial keys (which subsumes not-yet-scheduled roadmap item 3 and removes item 7's documented single_variable_slack positive-coefficient quirk); H3 fill-in-aware Markowitz-style entering-variable selection with a prefer-|coeff|=1 tie-break and partial pricing; H5 model-based phase selection via CaDiCaL's phase()/unphase() to keep item 8's win without its VSIDS-override regressions; H4 batched bound assertion deferring update() to item 6's existing quiescence point; H6 difference-logic fragment detection (Tier 1) with Cotton & Maler DL0-DL4 as the larger Tier 2. Recommended order: H2 -> H1 -> H3 -> H5 -> H4 -> H6.

summary.result: 64-bit kept. TM/p5-zenonumeric_s5 0.13s vs 0.13s (1.00x), sc-21.induction3 1.56 vs 1.55 (1.01x), uart-18.induction 0.57 vs 0.53 (1.08x), miplib/pp08a-12000 1.48 vs 1.59 (0.93x), DTP-Scheduling/constraints-tempo-width-30 7.59 vs 8.77 (0.87x) -- all five with ZERO promotions under both widths. clock_synchro/clocksynchro_2clocks 2.44s (32-bit) vs 1.10s (64-bit), 2.22x, with promotions 668,002 vs 358,801 and big-form operations 4,435,074 vs 364,834.
summary.interpretation: The trade-off is exactly the one predicted when the deviation was documented, now measured. Where coefficients stay small the widths are within noise or 32-bit is up to ~13% faster, because __int128 add/multiply are multi-instruction sequences where 64-bit ones are single instructions -- a cost paid on every operation. Where coefficients genuinely outgrow 32 bits, the wider fast path cuts big-form operations 12-fold and wins by 2.2x. A few percent on the common case buys a factor of two on the hard case.
summary.bug_found: Building the 32-bit variant immediately failed the existing representation_transitions unit test: Rational(std::int64_t) range-checked only `value >= -kSmallMax`, which is vacuous at kSmallMax == INT64_MAX (every std::int64_t satisfies it) but lets out-of-range values into the small form at any narrower width, violating the canonical-form invariant. Fixed in commit 251d29e. A latent bug in a knob nobody had turned yet.

entries.scope: docs/qf-lra-heuristics.md item H3: fill-in-aware entering-variable selection (PivotingRule::Sparse, commit cf491ce) and its promotion to the default together with the leaving-side half (commit dd60655). Includes the four-way 237-file promotion run that also settles item H1b, and the merge/campaign fuzz gates. pivot() rewrites every row in occurs_in_[entering] merging in a row of length |row(leaving)|, so a pivot's cost and the fill-in it creates are the Markowitz product of those two factors -- which none of Bland, Dantzig or SOI prices. entries.scope: Investigation of four truncated fuzz-gate shards during the milestone-wide campaign sweep (jobs 117248-117251), and the correction of a wrong first diagnosis. Recorded because the failure pattern looked exactly like a solver termination bug and was not one -- the next person to see a whole-shard timeout should not have to re-derive this.

environment.host: llm2smt-slurm; compute partition 9/9 allocated with 460+ jobs queued from other users during the failures

command.original: scripts/slurm_qfuf_fuzz_gate.sbatch, 6 fuzzsmt shards x 500 cases per configuration, --time=00:45:00
command.reruns: same shards resubmitted with --time=03:00:00 (jobs 117309-117312) and again at --time=02:00:00 (117333-117336)
command.isolation: srun on a compute node running fuzz_external.py directly with python3 -u, once writing to node-local /tmp and once to the same NFS fuzz-results tree the gate uses; plus the generator alone, and per-case timing/peak-RSS sweeps locally and remotely

summary.symptom: Four of the five sweep configurations reported 2500 of 3000 fuzzsmt cases, all otherwise clean (0 crashes, 0 wrong answers). One shard per job had hit the Slurm wall clock and been killed before fuzz_external.py writes summary.csv, so the shard vanished from the results rather than failing -- a truncated gate is indistinguishable from a clean one unless the summary count is checked.
summary.what_made_it_look_like_a_solver_bug: All four lost shards were the same FuzzSMT seed, 217251, across four DIFFERENT solver configurations (bland, dantzig, --no-lra-sparse-leaving, --no-lra-propagation), while the fifth job (row propagation), whose seed range skips 217251, completed every shard. It reproduced on a second run at a 3x longer wall limit, which produced zero case lines in three hours.
summary.why_it_is_not: The same seed completes 500/500 everywhere it was retried: locally in ~40s; on a compute node writing to node-local /tmp; and on a compute node writing to the same NFS fuzz-results tree the gate uses, in 126 seconds. Generation of its 500 files takes 0.33s locally and 0.61s remotely. Peak RSS across its cases is ~95MB for Primo and ~153MB for z3, against the 2G cgroup. Both the solver and the reference calls are already timeout-bounded at 5s inside fuzz_external.py, so a shard cannot exceed roughly COUNT * 2 * TIMEOUT = 83 minutes of solving -- the failures ran 180.
summary.conclusion: No solver hang. An environment/scheduling anomaly during a period when the cluster was saturated by other users' work; it did not reproduce once the queue drained. The cluster nodes are also 3-5x slower per case than the workstation (5 of the seed's cases exceed 8s remotely where only 1 hits the 5s cap locally), which narrows the margin but does not come close to explaining 180 minutes.
summary.corrected_diagnosis: An earlier commit (2b6e197) asserted the 45-minute limit was under the worst case 'by construction' and implied that was the cause. The arithmetic is right and the raise to two hours is kept as defence in depth, but it was NOT the cause here -- 83 minutes does not explain a 180-minute failure, and the shard actually completes in about two. The script comment has been corrected rather than left confidently wrong.

summary.headline: Solved of 595: z3 429 (72.1%), primo 373 (62.7%), cvc5 351 (59.0%). PAR2: z3 23138s, primo 29215s, cvc5 31766s. Primo beats cvc5 by 22 files and trails z3 by 56. ZERO cross-solver disagreements, zero crashes, zero errors, zero unsupported across all 595 files in all three solvers.
summary.correction_to_earlier_claims: On the 237-file stratified sample Primo had edged z3 168-167. That does NOT hold on an unseen set. The stratified sample -- assembled during this roadmap and used as its promotion bar -- was optimistic, which is exactly why the scrambled set was worth running.
summary.soundness_caveat: Scrambled benchmarks carry no (set-info :status), so bench_qf_uf_full.py's own wrong-answer column is inert here: it derives `expected` from :status and reports wrong=false for every row regardless of the answer. The zero-disagreement result above comes from scripts/compare_solver_answers.py comparing the three solvers against each other, which is the only soundness signal this set supports.
summary.gap_is_one_size_band: Solved by file size (primo / z3 / cvc5): 0-50KB 180/181/181 of 182; 50-500KB 142/134/122 of 191; 500KB-5MB 43/100/43 of 173; >5MB 8/14/5 of 49. Primo LEADS both references below 500KB and collapses above it, landing on exactly cvc5's number in the 500KB-5MB band. 18 files are solved only by Primo, 60 only by z3, 0 only by cvc5; 146 by nobody.
summary.not_a_preprocessing_size_problem: First hypothesis, and refuted by measurement. On four profiled gap instances Primo's prepared tableau matches z3's reported dimensions within ~5%: 9,315x11,633 vs 9,000x11,330; 8,960x10,479 vs 8,892x10,415; 4,822x5,405 vs 4,342x4,929; 24,976x27,016 vs 22,792x26,486. Primo also already folds the scrambler's (* 1.0 t)/(+ t 0.0) obfuscation -- verified directly, term size and solve-eqs counts identical with and without it. Both solvers build the same problem.
summary.diagnosis: The instances are dominated by Real equalities (8,226-40,820 lowered per file against 4,822-24,976 rows). Primo lowers t1=t2 to a pair of inequalities that item H1b puts on one shared slack, which then holds an upper and a lower bound at the same value -- a FIXED variable that Primo never exploits, leaving it a live pivotable row. z3 does exploit it: :arith-fixed-eqs 168-52,364 and :arith-offset-eqs 855-68,937 per instance, after which its search barely runs. On scrambled126657 z3 needs 9 decisions and 4 conflicts where Primo makes 141,124 decisions and 321M pivot term-operations. perf puts 86% of Primo's runtime in LraTableau::pivot, averaging 431 rows rewritten per pivot.
summary.timeout_caveat: z3's median time on the 76 files it wins and Primo loses is 25s of the 60s budget (max 57.9s), so it is near the boundary too. At 60s a 2x slower solver loses many files a longer budget would recover, and the competition's own timeout is 1200s -- this run may overstate the gap under competition conditions. Job 117414 re-runs exactly those 76 files at 600s to separate 'cannot' from 'needs more budget'.

Designed from the 2026-07-29 scrambled-competition profiling, which found these instances dominated by lowered Real equalities that item H1b puts on one shared slack. NOT PROMOTED: it did not clear the 595-file bar and ships opt-in behind --lra-fixed-elimination. Its row-freezing half was deleted outright.

entries.job_id: 117487 (scrambled, all 60 tasks COMPLETED), 117488 (stratified), 117585 (merge gate -- INVALID, see verification), 117589 (merge gate, 1000 cases, clean)

summary.headline: H7 does not clear its bar. Scrambled 595 at 60s: 373 solved with it off, 374 on, 375 with the freezing half disabled. PAR2 29204 / 29237 / 29195. Net +1 file on 595 with +19/-18 symmetric churn. Stratified 237 at 10s: 167 -> 168, PAR2 1559.1 -> 1531.7. Zero cross-solver disagreements on either set.
summary.the_mechanism_does_work: Local paired A/B is unambiguous per-instance: latendresse/ecoliFBAyicesTest-500 0.8s -> 0.1s (:lra.pivot-term-ops 8.66M -> 0.13M), scrambled335326 51.0s -> 14.9s (195M -> 27M), and roughly an order of magnitude less pivot work on instances that still time out. The diagnosis that these tableaus are dominated by fixed equality slacks is correct.
summary.but_it_is_bimodal: It does not generalize, and the band breakdown is what shows it. Solved by file size (H7-off / H7-on-without-freezing / z3): 0-50KB 177/179/178 of 179; 50-500KB 144/138/136 of 192; 500KB-5MB 45/45/101 of 174; >5MB 7/13/14 of 50. Per-band gain/loss for H7: 0-50KB +2/-0, 50-500KB +2/-8, 500KB-5MB +8/-8, >5MB +8/-2.
summary.where_the_gap_actually_is: The ENTIRE remaining 56-file deficit against z3 is the 500KB-5MB band (45 vs 101). H7 nets exactly zero there. Over the 32 files in that band both configurations solve in more than a second the MEDIAN is 0.64x -- the typical gap instance is 1.6x SLOWER -- with 17 files >20% slower against 8 files >25% faster. Overall median across all commonly-solved files is 0.94x.
summary.real_win_where_it_is_not_needed: The >5MB band is the one genuine gain: 7 -> 13 of 50, +8 gained against -2 lost, closing a 7-file deficit against z3's 14 down to 1. Among the 5 files both configurations solve there the median is 0.98x, so the gains are files crossing the 60s line rather than a broad speedup.
summary.methodological_correction: The four instances profiled to design H7 were all in the 500KB-5MB band, so the band choice was right -- but they were the winning tail of it, not a representative sample, and three of the four still timed out with H7 enabled. Presenting their 3.4x/8x as evidence the mechanism 'works' over-generalized from an instance selection biased toward the hypothesis under test. The band-level median (0.64x) is what caught it. Future gap work should profile the MEDIAN instance of the target band.
summary.freezing_deleted: The row-freezing half (drop a qualifying row from occurs_in_ so update()/check() skip it) was strictly negative: four files lost in the 500KB-5MB band against one gained elsewhere. It also carried all of H7's wrong-answer risk -- mark_boundable's caller contract, the throw enforcing it, the stale-assignment argument, the frozen-row-whose-term-later-became-basic case, RowDeactivationTrailEntry. Removed outright rather than left behind a flag: 352 lines deleted against 106 added (ebd2533). What remains has no wrong-answer mode; it is a pivot, which is what check() does on every repair.
summary.no_threshold_added: Deliberately did NOT add a size or row-length threshold to keep the >5MB win while dodging the mid-range cost. That is tuning a heuristic that lost its own bar -- item 8's recorded mistake.
summary.what_this_says_about_the_gap: The fixed-equality hypothesis is now tested and largely refuted for the band that holds the deficit. That is worth more than the +1 file: it removes the most plausible remaining explanation. Offset equalities (z3's :arith-offset-eqs, 855-68,937 per instance) remain untested.

verification.ablation_invariance: With H7 off, :sat.decisions and :lra.pivots are byte-identical to the pre-H7 build on the six-instance counter probe -- checked at eed259c and again after the demotion, so the shipped default is exactly pre-H7 behaviour.
verification.tests: Release and ASAN ctest green throughout. Unit tests pin: the elimination fires; the unbounded-candidate preference; that an already-fixed candidate is never pivoted INTO the basis (that guard was a real bug -- the other ranking criteria actively steer into picking one, and the test fails without it); conflict still found through an eliminated variable with every certificate literal genuinely asserted; push/pop across an elimination; verdict agreement with the ablation under both pivoting rules.
verification.mutation_checks: Before its removal, the freezing guard was mutation-checked both ways. Dropping it entirely made an existing end-to-end test return the wrong verdict (gaussian_elimination_can_be_disabled). Dropping only the mark_boundable half fired the throw immediately on real benchmarks (variable 1133 on scrambled335326, 1584 on ecoliFBAyicesTest-500). Both confirm the guard was load-bearing, which is why removing the feature it guarded was preferable to keeping both.
verification.fuzzing: 2100 fuzzsmt cases against z3 under ASAN with H7 enabled (300+300+1500, zero mismatches, timeouts only), plus an ASAN differential against the ablation over all 237 stratified files and the 60 smallest scrambled files: 0 sanitizer hits, 0 verdict mismatches. A further 1500-case ASAN campaign against z3 covers the shipped opt-in path specifically (--lra-fixed-elimination, freezing removed), since the earlier 2100 ran when H7 was default-on WITH freezing: 1428 PASS / 72 TIMEOUT, zero mismatches.
verification.invalid_gate: Job 117585 reported COMPLETED and had run ZERO cases: its only summary row was SKIPPED_MISSING_FUZZER. The gate script never put contrib/local/bin on PATH, relying on --export=ALL to inherit it from the submitting shell -- which works from an interactive shell but not from `ssh host bash -s` -- and fuzz_external.py treats a missing fuzzer as a skip with exit 0. Both fixed in 0524733 (PATH set inside the job; missing fuzzsmt/z3 now exits 2). Resubmitted as 117589. Recorded because a green job that tested nothing is the same class of error as the truncated shards of 117248-117251.
verification.merge_gate: Job 117589, the opt-in path (--lra-fixed-elimination) against build-slurm-rel: 1000 fuzzsmt QF_LRA cases over two shards, 997 PASS / 3 TIMEOUT, zero wrong answers against z3. Summary row counts checked against the 500-per-shard expectation before believing it, which is what caught 117585.

command.sources: Tim King, 'Effective Algorithms for the Satisfiability of Quantifier-Free Formulas Over Linear Real and Integer Arithmetic', PhD thesis, New York University, September 2014, https://cs.nyu.edu/media/publications/king_tim.pdf (sections 2.2.7 and 2.2.12); Bixby, 'Solving Real-World Linear Programs' (OR 2002) and Maros, 'Computational Techniques of the Simplex Method' (Springer 2003), both already in the survey; Wikipedia's revised simplex article for the Forrest-Tomlin / Bartels-Golub refactorization rationale.
command.note: The King PDF was read outside the repository and not committed, per the no-copyrighted-material-in-repo rule.

summary.retraction: Periodic refactorization does not transfer. In REVISED simplex the basis is an LU factorization updated per pivot, and those updates accumulate fill-in and numerical error beyond a fresh factorization -- that surplus is what refactorization discards. Primo stores the EXPLICIT tableau, which for a given basic/non-basic partition is B^-1 N and is uniquely determined: recomputing it from the original rows returns an identical matrix with identical density. The 5-17x densification measured in section 6.2 is a property of the basis reached, not recoverable garbage from the path taken to it. There is nothing to discard.
summary.lesson: 'Measured headroom' is only headroom if some mechanism can recover it. The 5-17x figure looked like an opportunity and was in fact a description of the problem. Retracted before any implementation effort, on a literature check that cost one session.
summary.h3_prior_art_correction: King section 2.2.12 records minimum-column-length entering selection, with a switch to Bland's rule past a finite cap, as the heuristic 'commonly used in implementations of SimplexForSMT', attributing it to MathSAT, OpenSMT, Yices, Yices 2, z3 and CVC4. That is item H3 and its anti-cycling fallback exactly. Our Monniaux (CAV 2009) citation remains accurate as a source but H3 must not be read as novel; the note and the LraTableau header now say so. The opt-in shortest-row LEAVING rule is the part with no counterpart described there -- King records Griggio's most-violated rule (CVC4, MathSAT5), which is our Dantzig choice.
summary.fill_in_not_addressed_in_smt_literature: King section 2.2.7 describes the explicit sparse tableau (entries linked into both a row list and a column list). Searching the thesis for fill-in, density, Markowitz and refactorization finds only that description -- no mechanism for controlling densification during search. The section 6.2 problem is not one this literature offers a ready answer to.

verification.claim_basis: The uniqueness of B^-1 N for a fixed basis is a property of the formulation, not an empirical finding; Primo's rows are maintained in exactly the basic = sum(coeff * nonbasic) form that makes it so.

entries.followups: Section 6.5 reordered: the cheapest remaining direction is evaluating the EXISTING opt-in row-based bound propagation on this band (a benchmark run, not an implementation). Revised simplex with an LU-factored basis is now listed explicitly as the representation change refactorization would require, with the observation that King records no Simplex-for-DPLL(T) implementation doing it. Monniaux's floating-point-guided basis selection is promoted for re-examination, since section 6.2 says the BASIS determines density and that is precisely what it chooses.

summary.step1_mechanism_is_real: Ablating smt.arith.propagate_eqs in z3: 3.1->6.9s (2.2x), 8.0->25.9s (3.2x), 19.7->62.8s (3.2x), and 26.1->21.1s (0.81x, i.e. HARMFUL) on the fourth. :arith-offset-eqs drops to zero when disabled, confirming the counter tracks this mechanism.
summary.step1_not_theory_combination: These are pure QF_LRA with no second theory, so the mechanism is not Nelson-Oppen equality propagation -- the usual purpose of implied equalities in SMT, and the outcome that would have made D3 worthless here. This was the specific risk the step was designed to test.
summary.step1_ceiling: Even with the mechanism disabled z3 solves all four in under 63s where Primo needs ~600s, so offset equalities are worth a few x of a 10-30x gap. D3 done perfectly would be valuable and would not close the band.
summary.step2_detection_is_free: Primo can detect these on H7's existing fixed-variable hook: a fixed basic variable whose row has two terms is a relation between two variables. Measured distinct pairs per instance: 591 / 3,224 / 1,519 / 4,721.
summary.step2_kills_the_expensive_design: Distinct eliminable columns are 369/5,694 (6.5%), 2,524/23,571 (10.7%), 778/26,041 (3.0%) and 4,032/17,286 (23.3%). Against z3's measured speedups the correlation is INVERTED: the instance with the most eliminable columns (23.3%) is the one where z3's mechanism hurts, and the one with the fewest (3.0%) gets the largest win. If the payoff came from shrinking the tableau it would track the eliminable share; it anti-correlates. So column merging is not the mechanism.
summary.design_redirected: The expensive interpretation (merge columns, eliminate a variable) needs a constant term in Row -- 17 internal term loops, 4 external consumers of row(), and the constant would participate in assignments and in Farkas certificates, so pivot(), update() and build_conflict() all change. That expense is not justified. The cheap interpretation fits the evidence: detect the relation and propagate bounds across it (x - y = c and x >= l gives y >= l - c), which needs no constant column and reuses both H7's detection hook and Primo's existing theory-propagation path. Scaled binary rows (a*x + b*y = c, a != -b) outnumber literal offset rows on two of four instances and are equally usable, so the opportunity is the binary-row count, not the narrower offset one.

verification.caveat: The anti-correlation is n=4 and suggestive rather than conclusive. It is enough to say the expensive design should not be built first, not enough to prove bound propagation is the whole mechanism.

summary.d1_and_d3_are_the_same_code: compute_implied_child_bound derives a bound on one row term from the basic variable's bound plus the remaining terms. For s = x - y with s fixed and x bounded that yields a bound on y -- exactly the cheap offset-equality mechanism D3 was redirected to. D1 and the useful part of D3 are the same implementation.
summary.the_feature_is_gated_off_where_it_is_nee: kBidirectionalRowPropagationMaxRowSize/MaxFanout are 32/32 and kRowBasedPropagation's are 64/64, all documented in-source as 'not precisely derived'. On these instances occurs_in reaches 521 and rows reach 91 terms, so bidirectional propagation fires only 11-68 times where the D3 census finds 7,000-190,000 binary rows.
summary.raising_the_caps_helps_and_is_non_monoto: scrambled228965: 9.6s (68 props) at 32/32, 6.5s (2,072) at 256/256, 32.8s (2,181) unlimited. scrambled312090: 61.6s (22), 58.5s (7,959), 64.3s (8,593). Unlimited is worse than 256 on both, so the caps do real work and are simply set an order of magnitude below what these instances need.
summary.headline: scrambled312090 is a gap file that times out at 60s in the default configuration and solves in ~58s with row propagation enabled at raised caps. That is the first direct evidence any of the section 6.5 directions moves a gap file.
summary.audit: Every --lra-* CLI option maps to a CheckSatOptions field and appears in the docs; no orphans in either direction. Three statistics (:lra.theory-checks, :lra.theory-conflicts, :lra.theory-decisions) were emitted but documented nowhere. docs/arithmetic.md now carries a full option table with defaults and a statistics table, including the :lra.pivots-is-not-comparable-across-an-H7-ablation caveat, and documents the four un-exposed propagation caps.
summary.citation_gap_closed: Item H7's header claimed it implemented 'the standard eliminate fixed variables step' with NO citation -- precisely the unsupported claim the paper-grounded rule exists to catch. Now cited to Andersen & Andersen, 'Presolving in linear programming', Mathematical Programming 71 (1995) 221-245, with the setting difference stated: presolve removes fixed variables once, before solving, from a problem whose bounds are all known, whereas H7 fires during search and must restore on backtracking. That difference is the likely reason H7 did not pay.

verification.instrumentation_reverted: The cap-override patch was reverted; git status clean, make check green.
verification.caveat: n=2, and 58.5s against a 60s budget is at this workstation's noise boundary. This justifies the cluster cap sweep, not a conclusion.

The cap *counts* it reports do reproduce -- raising the caps really does turn the mechanism on by 2-3 orders of magnitude -- so what is superseded is the timing conclusion, not the diagnosis that the feature is gated off where it would be needed.

entries.scope: Direction D1's cap sweep: does row-based/bidirectional bound propagation, run with caps large enough to actually fire, move the 500KB-5MB gap band? Plus the merge-tier fuzz gate for the raised-cap configuration.

environment.binary: build-slurm-rel/primo (Release, cadical-3.0.0-7b99c07), verified at git 50ad2dd by slurm_prepare_benchmark_workspace.py --check-only before submission
environment.notes: The four propagation caps became CheckSatOptions fields in commit 2e1eb55 specifically so this sweep could vary them per run rather than per build; the 2026-07-30 entry's numbers came from a rebuild per data point.

command.sweep: sbatch scripts/slurm_qf_lra_row_propagation_sweep.sbatch -- job 117726, 5 configurations x 20 shards = 100 array tasks, all COMPLETED, 20/20 shard CSVs present per configuration

benchmark.timeout_rationale: The manifest is defined as the files z3 solves at 60s and Primo does not, so at 60s the baseline solves 0 of 59 by construction and every configuration is scored against zero. At 300s a majority already solves (section 6.1a: 45/59 at 600s, median 167s), so the sweep compares per-file times.

summary.result: REJECTED. Solved counts: base 37, rp-default 34, rp-128 37, rp-256 36, rp-1024 36 of 59. No cap setting beats the baseline; the best is a tie. PAR2 19465 / 19719 / 18155 / 19294 / 18591.
summary.median_speedup_is_real_but_does_not_conv: Median paired speedup over files both configurations solve in >1s rises with the caps: 1.01x, 1.20x, 1.14x, 1.30x (n=30-33). Every configuration nonetheless loses about as many files as it gains (+3/-6, +4/-4, +5/-6, +6/-7), and the gained and lost files are different files.
summary.the_mechanism_definitely_ran: Raising the caps turns propagation on by 2-3 orders of magnitude on this band. scrambled312090 bidirectional propagations 21 -> 7,959 (256) -> 8,419 (1024), row-based 213,354 -> 904,275 -> 955,787; scrambled228965 bidirectional 55 -> 2,072 -> 2,719. This is a mechanism firing 380x harder and still not moving the band, not a null result from code that never fired.
summary.the_motivating_instance_does_not_reprodu: scrambled312090 was the whole case for D1: locally 61.6s at default caps against 58.5s at 256, i.e. a gap file crossing a 60s budget. On the cluster it is 143s at baseline against 139s at 256 -- a 3% difference, with both figures more than double the local ones. The 2026-07-30 entry's own caveat (n=2, at a 60s boundary, workstation timing unreliable that session) was correct and is the explanation. scrambled228965 does reproduce (67s -> 13s at 256, a genuine 5x) but 1024 makes it worse than baseline (101s).
summary.churn_signature: scrambled178771 (222s at baseline) and scrambled21782 (148s) are lost by every configuration. scrambled11414 is gained by every configuration but lands anywhere from 48s to 244s depending on caps. That spread is churn at the timeout boundary, not a systematic effect.
summary.not_ruled_out: A per-instance or adaptive cap policy. The 5x on scrambled228965 and the 1.30x median are real; something that could identify those instances in advance would collect them. That is a materially larger item than the one closed here and is not pursued on this evidence -- the precedent is item H7, rejected rather than tuned after its own bar came back flat.
summary.soundness: Zero cross-configuration answer disagreements over the 59 files (the scrambled set carries no :status, so cross-configuration disagreement is the only soundness signal available from it) and zero wrong answers reported.
summary.fuzz_gate: Job 117767: 2,000 fuzzsmt QF_LRA cases against z3 on the 1024-cap configuration, 4/4 shard summaries present, 0 wrong answers, 1,976 PASS + 24 TIMEOUT at the 5s per-case budget. All 24 timeouts were re-checked individually against the default configuration: none is a soundness disagreement, 12 are unknown under both configurations even at a longer budget, and 3 differ only in whether one configuration finished within the budget.
summary.gate_limitation: The fuzz gate ran the Release build, not build-slurm-fuzz: the remote ASAN toolchain is still broken (head node lacks libasan, compute nodes lack C++ headers). This gate therefore carries no sanitizer coverage and must not be read as if it did.
summary.also_closes_d3: This sweep closes direction D3 (offset-equality detection + bound propagation) as well, which was not noticed when the result was first written up. D3's redirected cheap design -- 'detect x - y = c and propagate bounds across it' -- IS compute_implied_child_bound, as D1's own finding (a) already recorded ('D1 and the useful part of D3 are the same code'). Binary rows have size 2 so no row-size cap ever excluded them, and at caps 1024 the fanout gate is effectively off, so the sweep ran D3's design at full reach on the whole band. D3's expensive column-merge design was already rejected on the 2026-07-30 anti-correlation census.
summary.residual_d3_gap_not_tested: One piece of D3 the sweep did NOT test: a trigger, not a computation. D3 proposed firing on H7's hook -- the moment a basic variable becomes fixed. D1's code fires only on a bound change to a variable occurring as a nonbasic term, and pivot() clears occurs_in_[entering_var], so a basic variable occurs in nothing and a bound change on it scans nothing. When the equality fixing s is asserted after x already has its bound, the implied bound on y is not derived until one of that row's terms moves again. Cheap to close, but the sweep argues against expecting it to pay: it buys more firing, and 21 -> 8,419 firings moved nothing. Recorded, not built.

entries.docs: docs/qf-lra-heuristics.md section 6.5, D1's outcome subsection and the ranked table.

entries.scope: Is there work other than Monniaux CAV 2009 on floating-point-guided basis selection for an exact simplex in SMT? Prompted by D2 being named the next direction after D1/D3 closed.

environment.notes: Web search plus two papers read in full (KBT FMCAD 2014, and the PAAR 2012 abstract/results). PDFs read outside the repo and not committed, per the no-copyrighted-material rule.

summary.answer: Yes -- the technique has been implemented at least twice more since Monniaux, both in SMT solvers, and both report far smaller gains than D2 was scoped for.
summary.king_barrett_tinelli_2014: FMCAD 2014, CVC4 + GLPK 4.52. Their SeedExact procedure pivots the exact tableau toward the LP solver's final basic set, and the paper explicitly equates it to Monniaux's ForcedPivot. Two design points we did not have: (1) BalancedSolve calls the exact solver FIRST under a 200-pivot cap and only falls back to the LP solver when that cap is exceeded, so it is a fallback for hard theory calls rather than a preprocessing phase -- this dissolves D2's Risk B, since bounds are known mid-search; (2) ImportAssignment converts the LP solver's float assignment back to rationals by Diophantine approximation with denominators capped at 2^26. Measured QF_LRA payoff: 645 of 652 against plain CVC4's 636, i.e. +9 files, all from the miplib family, which is internally mixed integer/real so the gain runs through the MIP path rather than the LP force-pivot path.
summary.de_oliveira_monniaux_2012: PAAR 2012, OpenSMT, the direct continuation of CAV 2009: LP called first, result seeds the exact search. 14% faster overall (4h44m45s against 5h26m55s over 634 benchmarks), with 11 of 634 (1.7%) showing at least one float/exact disagreement -- rare, but why the exact solver must verify.
summary.earlier_work: Faure, Nieuwenhuis, Oliveras & Rodriguez-Carbonell (SAT 2008) integrated several LP solvers into Barcelogic with lazy exact checking; Yu & Malik (SAT 2006) used an LP solver as a theory solver without addressing incorrect results.
summary.the_sentence_that_recalibrates_d2: KBT's own summary of all prior studies: existing SMT solvers outperform the LP-augmented versions on SMT-LIB benchmarks, EVEN IF the LP solver results are not checked for correctness, because solving requires many related but individually simple theory calls. Their balanced control structure is what makes the technique pay at all.
summary.consequence_for_d2: Section 6.1a says this band needs 2x for 15 files and 5x for 37. The literature offers ~14% overall and +9 files on a 652-file set. D2 is not a 10-30x technique and its entry has been rescoped accordingly -- still open, but no longer described as 'large'.
summary.cvc5_has_no_glpk: Measured: contrib/local/bin/cvc5 1.3.4 --show-config reports 'glpk : no'. The reference cvc5 therefore carries none of CVC4's LP integration, so its 9-of-59 on the mid-band gap is not evidence about this technique in either direction. Worth knowing before anyone reads cvc5's weakness there as a verdict on LP-guided simplex.

entries.docs: docs/papers/lra-related-work.md (new 'Floating-point-guided exact simplex' subsection) and docs/qf-lra-heuristics.md section 6.5's D2 entry (Risk C, and the ranked table's expected-size column).

entries.scope: First flat profile of the 500KB-5MB mid-band gap files at the current commit. Prompted by the question of whether gprof had ever been run on the lagging instances -- it had not: the only QF_LRA flat profile on record was perf on constraints-tempo-width-30 at 35878c4 (before H1/H2/H3/H7), and the 2026-07-30 'post-H7 gap profiling' entry used counters and throwaway instrumentation rather than a profiler.

environment.binary: build-gprof/primo (RelWithDebInfo -pg -O2 -g) for gprof; build/primo (Release) for the allocator measurement
environment.notes: perf is unusable in this sandbox -- kernel.perf_event_paranoid=4 and sysctl is permission-denied -- and valgrind is not installed, so compile-time instrumentation was the only available profiler. -pg penalises call-heavy code, so gprof rankings are sound but absolute percentages are indicative.

command.gprof: cmake -B build-gprof -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS='-pg -O2 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer' -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS=-pg; then build-gprof/primo --quiet <instance>; gprof -b -p / -q build-gprof/primo gmon.out
command.allocator: LD_PRELOAD of a throwaway wrapper (scratchpad only, not committed) around malloc/free/realloc/calloc accumulating rdtsc cycles, run against the Release binary -- gprof samples only the executable's text segment and cannot see libc

summary.allocator_is_retired: THE headline. The 2026-07-27 perf profile that motivated item H2 put ~42% of runtime in the allocator and ~12% in GMP copy/init. On the gap band at the current commit it is 6.0% and 4.0% (9.78M and 16.94M malloc/free pairs). H2 did what it was built for. Anyone reading the older profile would still rank the allocator first; it should not be.
summary.pivot_dominates: LraTableau::pivot is 61.0% self on scrambled339450 (3,706 calls) and 85.4% on scrambled228965 (11,647 calls, 1.96 ms/call). No hidden hotspot anywhere else.
summary.confirms_section_6_2: Section 6.2's fill-in diagnosis was derived entirely from counters (:lra.pivot-row-updates, :lra.pivot-term-ops) and had never been checked against a profiler. It holds.
summary.direction_setting: Positive evidence that no misplaced overhead remains to reclaim: after rebuild_occurs_in_index and the allocator, the rest is pivot doing real arithmetic. The remaining gap needs an algorithmic change (fewer or cheaper pivots), not tuning -- the same conclusion D1's rejection reached from the other side.
summary.lead_1_rebuild_occurs_in_index: Consistently second at 7.5% / 4.4%. Its CALL COUNT is already fixed (the 2026-07-27 item-0 follow-up cut it from once-per-undone-pivot to once-per-pop, -97%; counts here are 522/526 and 3,870/3,874, so that holds). What remains is that each call is a full O(vars_.size()) rebuild and these instances have ~26,000 variables -- about 3.8ms per call. Making it incremental over the undone trail entries is a different fix from the one already applied.
summary.lead_2_sort_should_be_a_merge: 11.6% on scrambled339450 (but only 1.6% on scrambled228965, so instance-dependent) is the sort-merge in pivot's affected-row loop. combine_scratch_ concatenates the affected row's terms with the scaled entering row's terms and std::sorts the result, but both halves are already ordered by variable id -- this is a merge, not a sort. Must first check whether rows are ordered on every path into that loop; the candidate-selection site's comment says a Row is not sorted by var id.
summary.symbol_name_caveat: gprof reports a hot vector<SoiBreakPoint>::_M_realloc_insert, which is impossible under the default Sparse rule since soi_select() is gated behind rule_ == PivotingRule::Soi. Its call-graph parent is the introsort inside pivot, so this is COMDAT folding of identically-generated template code, not SOI running by default. Checked rather than assumed, because a hot SOI symbol in a non-SOI run would read as a real bug.

entries.followups: Neither lead is implemented. Both are hot-path changes to LraTableau and would need a fuzz gate plus a Slurm A/B before being described as wins.

entries.scope: Item H8: pivot()'s affected-row loop merges two ordered rows instead of concatenating and sorting them. Found by the 6.2a flat profile. Includes the incremental occurs_in_ experiment that was built alongside it and rejected.

environment.binary: build-slurm-rel/primo at e6020ca; baseline is a second worktree built at the parent commit 03c28da, so the A/B is same-node and same-time
environment.notes: Local paired A/Bs were run interleaved base/new per instance, two reps each, after an earlier round in this project produced sign-flipped timings from measuring while builds competed for CPU.

summary.change: pivot()'s affected-row loop was O(m log m) per affected row: it concatenated the affected row's terms with the scaled entering row's terms into combine_scratch_ and std::sorted the result. Both halves are already ordered by var id, so it is a linear merge. Rows were only incidentally ordered, so this makes it an invariant on Row (add_row sorts; pivot splices basic_var into new_entering_row at its ordered position instead of prepending). Two smaller wins follow: the zero check is needed only in the equal-var-id branch, and the affected row is taken by reference and moved into the trail instead of copied twice.
summary.midband_result: base 37 solved / PAR2 19475, H8 38 solved / PAR2 18309. Median paired speedup 1.16x over the 37 files both solve in >1s (p25 1.13, p75 1.22). Churn +1/-0.
summary.stratified_result: base 189 solved / PAR2 6473, H8 192 solved / PAR2 6067. Median paired 1.23x over 67 files >1s (p25 1.10, p75 1.33). Churn +3/-0.
summary.no_regressions: Zero regressions on either bar -- churn is one-directional on both, which no other item in the heuristics note has managed. The p25-p75 span of 1.10-1.33 says this is a uniform constant-factor win, not a few instances carrying an average.
summary.soundness: Zero cross-configuration answer disagreements and zero wrong answers on both benchmark runs (the stratified sample carries :status, so its wrong-answer column is live, unlike the scrambled set's).
summary.fuzz_gates: Campaign tier on the default path: 3000 fuzzsmt QF_LRA cases, 6/6 shard summaries, 2980 PASS / 20 TIMEOUT, 0 wrong. Mutation tasks (job 117932): opfuzz 14/14 seeds valid with 5,448 solver calls, two yinyang typefuzz shards 14/14 valid with 2,748 and 2,744 calls, 0 bug triggers and 0 bug files across all three. Merge tier on the SOI path: 1000 fuzzsmt cases, 2/2 summaries, 943 PASS / 57 TIMEOUT, 0 wrong. Release build -- the remote ASAN toolchain is still broken, so none of this carries sanitizer coverage.
summary.summarizer_caveat: scripts/summarize_fuzz_results.py reports opfuzz/yinyang as summaries=0 cases=0 because those stages do not write a fuzz_external.py-style summary.csv. That is a summarizer limitation, not a gate that ran nothing -- verified from the task logs (seed counts, solver-call counts, 0 bug triggers) and by finding zero files under the bugs directories. Do not read that 0 as a failure, and do not read it as a pass without checking the logs.
summary.rejected_incremental_occurs_in: The profile's other lead, rebuild_occurs_in_index() at 8%, was also built and then reverted. Instrumentation split its cost exactly: clear pass 0.05s, fill 1.65s over 138M scattered push_backs into 57,658 separate heap vectors. Since a pop restores only ~384 rows of 47,148, patching occurs_in_ per restored row inside undo() looked like ~100x less work. Measured, it is 1.4-1.8x SLOWER (0.88, 0.97, 0.55, 0.61, 0.70, 0.71, 0.62, 0.60 across four instances, two reps). Two compounding errors in the estimate: the cost scales with pivots undone (3,706), not pops (522); and dropping a listing is a std::remove scan of occurs_in_[var], not O(1), over rows averaging ~1,048 terms per row update. A full rebuild of a cheap index beats a targeted patch of an expensive one. The only fix that would actually help is a CSR-style representation for occurs_in_, which touches 29 call sites and should be considered as part of D4 rather than on its own.

command.census: count prepared-tableau variables that are the bound_var of no arithmetic PreparedAtom (the paper's 'does not occur in any elementary atom'), split by basic/non-basic, plus the number of rows holding at least one such variable

summary.result: Free variables are 0.5-4.3% of the tableau: scrambled339450 2,503 of 57,658 (4.3%), scrambled312090 119 of 26,041 (0.46%), scrambled228965 28 of 5,694 (0.5%).
summary.why_it_is_worse_than_the_share_suggests: Those few variables are spread across nearly every row -- 43,140 of the rows on scrambled339450 (91%), 17,812 on scrambled312090, 2,999 on scrambled228965 hold at least one. The elimination is Gaussian, so substituting them out rewrites all those rows and generates fill-in, which section 6.2 identifies as the bottleneck. Shrinking the matrix by 4% while densifying 91% of its rows is not a trade this band can afford.
summary.sanity_check: Every free variable found was non-basic (basic count zero on all three instances), which is the expected shape: a slack exists only because some polynomial carried an atom, so slacks always have bounds, and the free variables are exactly the structural ones that never got a direct bound. A nonzero basic count would have meant the census was measuring the wrong thing.
summary.supersedes_an_inference: The prior reasoning -- H1a already removed the trivial slack rows, and prepared dimensions match z3's within ~5% -- pointed the same way but was an inference. This is a direct count.
summary.conclusion: TR Section 3.1 presimplification stays unimplemented, now on measured rather than inferred grounds. With it closed, no technique from the base paper remains unimplemented for QF_LRA.

summary.mechanism: Not undoing pivots means the search keeps the repair work it already paid for. Pivot counts drop 2.3-5.3x on the profiled instances (scrambled228965 11,647 -> 3,460; scrambled339450 3,706 -> 1,629; scrambled365036 122,026 -> 22,926), and gprof shows rebuild_occurs_in_index gone from the profile entirely since nothing structural changes on a pop.
summary.THIS IS NOT A FREE WIN: Unlike item H8, the churn is two-directional: +32/-11 on the 595 set and +7/-2 on the stratified sample. Among the 145 commonly-solved files taking more than a second, 62 are >10% SLOWER and 64 are >10% faster -- median paired speedup is 1.01x with p25 0.63 and p75 1.30. The tails are large in both directions (max 24.9x, min 0.10x; worst case scrambled31749 at 2.5s -> 24.0s). It nets +21 because the wins land on instances near the timeout while most of the losses do not.
summary.regression_shape: 10 of the 11 lost files were already taking 24-60s against a 60s budget, so they were marginal before. The 32 gained files solve at a median of 27.9s.
summary.why_the_variance: Inherent to the design rather than a defect: keeping the basis across a backtrack keeps a basis that was good for the *previous* subproblem. Sometimes that is a warm start, sometimes it is a worse starting point than the initial all-slack basis would have been.
summary.bearing_on_d2: This is the first direct evidence on our own solver that the starting basis matters enormously -- 10x in either direction on the same instance, from nothing but which basis the search happens to inherit. That is the premise D2 (floating-point-guided basis selection) rests on, and it had not previously been measured here.
summary.soi_excluded: PivotingRule::Soi keeps the old scheme: its objective row is a sum over the currently violated rows, not a linear combination of A, so neither half of the soundness argument covers it.

command.counter_check: temporary counters around the std::remove in pivot's affected-row loop, measured then reverted

summary.distribution: On scrambled228965, 262.5 billion instructions total: 70.4% in stl_algobase.h attributed to LraTableau::pivot, 11.1% stl_iterator.h, 9.8% predefined_ops.h -- about 91% inside pivot, and almost none of it arithmetic (Rational::operator* is ~1%, libc _int_malloc 0.22%).
summary.what_it_actually_is: One linear-scan algorithm: the std::remove that drops other_basic from occurs_in_[var]. Counted directly rather than inferred from symbol names, because attribution has misled here before (6.2a's COMDAT folding). scrambled228965: 40.1M calls scanning 37.6 BILLION elements, average 938 per call. scrambled339450: 51.5M calls, 25.9 billion elements, average 504.
summary.the_fix_that_follows: Most of that work is immediately undone: the loop removes other_basic from every term's occurrence list and then re-adds it for every term of the rebuilt row, and after H8's merge most terms are in both. Both rows are ordered by var id (the Row invariant H8 established), so the true delta is one linear pass -- a term carried over unchanged needs no occurrence update at all, and only terms genuinely entering (from the entering row) or leaving (cancelled to zero, or entering_var itself) need one.
summary.significance: This is larger than anything left in section 6.5's direction list, and unlike D2 or D4 it is contained, additive, and rests on an invariant that already exists. Not attempted yet.
summary.allocator_still_retired: libc _int_malloc is 0.22% of instructions, confirming the 2026-07-31 finding that H2 retired the allocator as a target; it has not crept back.

entries.scope: Item H10: maintain occurs_in_ by delta instead of a remove-and-re-add round trip per affected row. The target callgrind identified as ~91% of instructions.

entries.scope: Audit of what the two QF_LRA fuzzers actually cover, prompted by the question 'is our fuzzing based on all the different families we have?'. The answer was no, in two independent ways: the mutation seed corpus held 3 of the division's 17 families, and every FuzzSMT run in this project's history used QF_LRA's stock default parameters.

environment.binary: build/primo at c29ed09 (Release), fuzzsmt 0.3 and z3 5.0.0 from contrib/local
environment.notes: Parameter measurements are local and single-seed unless stated; they are throughput/size measurements, not performance claims.

command.size_ladder: for each setting: fuzzsmt QF_LRA -seed <s> <args> -bulk-export 10..150, then build/primo -q on each output
command.differential: python3 scripts/fuzz_external.py --fuzzer fuzzsmt --solver './build/primo --quiet' --refs z3 --logic QF_LRA --count 150 --timeout 10 --seed 777 --fuzzer-args <profile> --out <dir>, for profiles 1-3

summary.seed_corpus_gap: benchmarks/seeds/qf_lra_real held 14 files from check, DTP-Scheduling and keymaera, plus gasburner which is not in the division at all. 14 of 17 families had never been mutation-fuzzed, including latendresse (pure LP, zero decisions, very large pivot counts) and LassoRanker (419 files, the largest source of Primo's lead) -- the shapes items H8, H9 and H10 each rewrote.
summary.fuzzsmt_parameter_gap: Every QF_LRA gate in this log ran '-ms 1 -Ms 3 -mv 1 -Mv 3 -mf 1 -mp 1 -ma 1 -Ma 2'. For QF_LRA that is FuzzSMT's stock default: -ms/-Ms are sort counts and -mf/-mp/-ma/-Ma are function/predicate/arity knobs, applied only to the QF_UF* logics and silently ignored here. Effective settings were -Mv 3, -Mc 3, -Mbw 4, so every generated case had at most three Real variables and every coefficient in [1,15] -- the GMP bignum paths in DeltaRational and Farkas combination were never generated.
summary.measured_costs: -Mbw 16 free (max literal 15 -> 54430, no size or time cost); -Mc 10 3x file size; -Mv 15 9x; -ref 2 7x; -ref 3 20x with generation itself hitting the wall; -Mv 15 -ref 2 composes to ~2MB per case. -Mv 5 -Mc 4 -Mbw 16 costs 18s/100 cases with 1% timeouts and is the chosen mid tier.
summary.bool_layer: -bool-and yields 100% unsat and -bool-or 100% sat, both at ~4s/100 cases, against ~11% unsat for the random layer. -bool-cnf is unusable: FuzzSMT 0.3 emits a malformed let block and z3 rejects the output too ('invalid let declaration'); all 150 cases were correctly rejected by Primo's parser.
summary.differential_result: 450 cases across profiles 1-3 against z3: 449 PASS, 1 timeout, zero answer disagreements and zero crashes.

caveats: The first measurement suggested -Mbw 16 was 5x CHEAPER than -Mbw 4 (4.2s vs 22.7s per 150 cases) and doubled the unsat rate. A second seed gave 3.4s vs 3.7s and no unsat difference: FuzzSMT's output is seed-driven and changing a parameter changes the random stream, so per-setting sizes wander. The defensible claim is that -Mbw 16 costs nothing, not that it wins.
This is a coverage widening, not a bug hunt that found something. No defect was found by any of it.

command.job: sbatch --array=6-10 scripts/slurm_qfuf_fuzz_gate.sbatch with PRIMO_FUZZ_OPFUZZ_SEEDS/PRIMO_FUZZ_YINYANG_SEEDS=benchmarks/seeds/qf_lra_division, OPFUZZ_ITERATIONS=300, YINYANG_ITERATIONS=200, WALL_SECONDS=5400, timeouts 20s, no fuzzsmt shards

summary.result: All five tasks: '34 seeds processed, 22 valid, 12 invalid / 0 bug triggers found'. Zero entries in every bugs/ directory.
summary.why_superseded: The 12 'invalid' seeds were not malformed. typefuzz's -L is a seed FILE-SIZE limit, 20000 bytes by default in scripts/yinyang_fuzz.sh, and it drops oversized seeds silently. The 12 dropped seeds are exactly the 12 corpus files over 20 KB: tropical-matrix (160/180 KB), latendresse (125 KB), TM (77/81 KB), 2017-Heizmann (73/78 KB), miplib (70 KB) and LassoRanker (45 KB). The corpus had just been widened from 3 families to 17 and this cut it back to 11, discarding latendresse and LassoRanker -- the two families the widening existed to cover.
summary.verification: Confirmed per seed by running typefuzz -i 1 on each of the 34 seeds individually on the cluster: the 12 that report '0 valid, 1 invalid' are exactly the 12 over 20000 bytes, and the 22 that do not are all under.

caveats: An earlier hypothesis -- that YinYang discards seeds whose reference answer times out -- was WRONG. It only looked right because the oversized files are also the ones z3 cannot answer quickly. The per-seed run distinguished the two.

Separately and still true: at a 20s reference timeout z3 5.0.0 does not answer the unmutated LassoRanker, latendresse, miplib or tropical-matrix seeds at all, so even with the size limit raised those iterations cannot yield a verdict without a longer --solver-timeout.
entries.outcome: Fixed in 22409b1: the gate now passes --file-size-limit 200000 (matching build_fuzz_seed_corpus.py's --max-bytes) and yinyang_fuzz.sh names oversized seeds on stderr before starting. A replacement campaign is required before citing mutation-fuzz coverage of the widened corpus.

summary.protocol_root_cause: CaDiCaL 3.0's factor/BVA machinery can introduce internal extension variables. Incremental clients that add more user variables after solve must use declare_more_variables() when available; Primo previously grew max_var with resize()/reserve(), which can collide with CaDiCaL-owned extension variables and causes CaDiCaL to abort by design.
summary.implemented_fix: CMake now detects CaDiCaL::Solver::declare_more_variables; sat::CadicalBackend::new_var() uses it when available and falls back to resize()/reserve() only for older CaDiCaL versions.
summary.local_repro: The three default-run cpachecker-induction aborts from the broader 100-instance SLURM comparison no longer abort locally with default CaDiCaL options: two return unknown under a 15s timeout and one returns sat.
summary.fuzz: 1000 generated mixed QF_UFLRA cases, seed 20260802, timeout 5s: PASS 1000, wrong 0, crash 0, reference disagreements 0.

entries.outcome: Accepted and committed as 8e88eef. The protocol abort is fixed locally and covered by a SAT-backend regression test plus QF_UFLRA differential fuzzing. A fresh SLURM broader-sample rerun is still needed before replacing the previous 6799453 performance table.

environment.binary: build-profile/primo at eea5164, RelWithDebInfo, PRIMO_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS=OFF for profiling-only GCC 13 build; build-gprof/primo at eea5164 with -pg

callgrind.online_top_inclusive: lra_implied_real_equalities accounts for 12,983,637,602 instructions, 89.74% of online total.

gprof_online.hot_call_counts: lra_assignment_conflicts_with_extra_atom 6450 calls, PreparedLraTheory constructor 6517 calls, LraTableau::check 7005 calls

entries.outcome: The online regression is not parsing/preprocessing and not primarily the paired-bound callback producer. Online precreation and propagated interface equalities increase SAT arrangement traffic, which causes repeated final mixed checks. Each final LRA-to-EUF scan calls lra_implied_real_equalities, which checks all shared Real pairs by rebuilding an augmented LRA theory for lhs < rhs and rhs < lhs. On the solved MathSAT profile case this all-pairs scan dominates callgrind at 89.74% of instructions; gprof independently shows thousands of augmented LRA preparations and tableau checks. The next design decision is whether online mode should skip or cap this broader final LRA equality mining, or replace it with cached/reused LRA equality evidence, while retaining the narrow paired-bound online producer.
